title: How Clean Is Your Car
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article opens with NASCAR crew chief Chad Knaus's unusual hiring habit of checking a candidate's car in the parking lot after an interview, using how well they maintain their vehicle as a proxy for how they'll care for his equipment and team. It generalizes this into a broader observation about leaders who rely on small symbolic signals, like a cluttered workspace, to make inferences about character traits such as organization or reliability. The piece acknowledges such shortcuts can be biased or unfair, but argues good judges of talent inevitably lean on some personal heuristics, and invites readers to name their own.
points: NASCAR crew chief Chad Knaus reportedly judges candidates partly by how well they maintain their own car.
The anecdote illustrates leaders using small symbolic signals as proxies for character traits.
The piece acknowledges such inferences can be unfair or biased, while noting they're nearly universal.
Readers are prompted to identify their own personal 'tell' for evaluating prospective team members.
quotes: A NASCAR crew chief’s success relies heavily on the capabilities and performance of their team.
He doesn’t care what kind of car they drive (old, new, flashy, expensive, or modified). He only wants to know one thing—do they take care of it?
If the car isn’t clean and well-maintained, Knaus turns the candidate down. He figures if you don’t take care of your stuff, you aren’t going to take good care of his.

For instance, what if you walked into a prospective candidate’s workspace and saw stacks of papers, boxes, and trash? Would the assumption that they were disorganized and likely to have cluttered thinking be fair and important?
Others may argue that they are biased in their judgments over their inferences, but almost every good judge of talent relies on some.
